reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: A large-calibre submucosal artery that fails to taper normally and erodes through a tiny mucosal defect, causing brisk arterial bleeding
Most commonly found in the proximal stomach along the lesser curve within a few centimetres of the gastro-oesophageal junction, but described throughout the gut
Classically presents as recurrent, obscure, or massive haematemesis and melaena out of proportion to the minimal surrounding mucosal abnormality
The lesion is easily missed because the surrounding mucosa is normal and bleeding is often intermittent, so a high index of suspicion and repeat endoscopy may be needed
Endoscopic haemostasis is first-line and often combines a mechanical method (clips or band ligation) with thermal or injection therapy
Marking the site with a tattoo or clip aids relocation if bleeding recurs or surgery is required
Angiographic embolisation or surgical wedge resection is reserved for endoscopic failure
reference.pathophysiology: A Dieulafoy lesion is an abnormally large, tortuous submucosal artery that retains a wide calibre as it approaches the mucosal surface instead of tapering into a capillary bed. Pulsatile pressure and possibly local mucosal thinning lead to erosion of a pinpoint mucosal defect overlying the vessel, exposing the artery and allowing sudden, often torrential arterial haemorrhage. Because the surrounding mucosa is otherwise normal and there is no ulcer or mass, the lesion can be extremely difficult to identify, particularly between bleeding episodes when it may not be actively spurting.
additionalDifferentials: Bleeding peptic ulcer with a visible vessel
Aortoenteric fistula in the appropriate setting
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, repeated if necessary, to identify active spurting or an adherent clot over normal mucosa
Endoscopic tattoo or clip placement to mark the lesion for future localisation
Computed tomography angiography or catheter angiography when endoscopy is unrevealing during active bleeding
Tagged red-cell scintigraphy for intermittent obscure bleeding
Full blood count, coagulation profile, and group-and-save or crossmatch
Capsule endoscopy or enteroscopy for lesions in the small bowel
redFlags: Massive haematemesis with haemodynamic instability requiring resuscitation
Recurrent obscure bleeding with negative initial endoscopy
Rebleeding after apparently successful endoscopic therapy
reference.prognosis: With prompt endoscopic haemostasis the outlook is generally good and definitive control is achieved in most patients, though the lesion has a notable tendency to rebleed, and mortality rises when diagnosis is delayed or bleeding is massive.
pitfalls: Dismissing normal-looking mucosa and overlooking the tiny bleeding point
Failing to mark the site, making relocation difficult if bleeding recurs
Relying on a single endoscopy when bleeding is intermittent
Delaying angiography or surgery after repeated endoscopic failure
